This indicates that discrepant fatigue limits may be due to discrepant form. 
There is also another point to be noted. 
If, during a fatigue test of the usual 
type, the machine is stopped when slips have begun to develop, they will heal 
themselves during the period of rest and so confuse the final result. 
There 
are therefore several causes which together act to modify the results of a test 
on the fatigue limit of a material by the method of repeated oscillations.
I think that a fatigue limit of practical value can be determined from 
a looping test of the type described in my recent paper. 
That is to say, 
the load is applied and removed, and then reapplied and removed through a 
wider range, until at last a range is found at which looping appears. 
When 
this loop appears the fatigue range has just been passed. 
I have shown in my 
recent paper that an iron or mild-steel bar, when tested in this way, and when 
loops corresponding to considerable overstrain have been described, will show 
an elastic line again when re-tested again after a rest. 
(See Curve 5, sheet 1, 
“ Phil. Trans. ” (1920).) 
But this process does not alter the real fatigue limit 
■of the material, as can be seen from the curves.

A Study oj Catalytic Actions at Solid Surfaces. 
X .— The Interaction 
of Carbon Monoxide and Hydrogen as conditioned by Nickel at 
relatively Low Temperatures.— A Practical Synthesis of Methane.
By E. F. A rmstrong, D.Sc., F.R.S., and T. P. H ilditch, D.Sc.
(Received December 19, 1922.)
The investigation described in this communication had for its primary 
object the production of formaldehyde or methyl alcohol. In this aim we 
have been so far unsuccessful, but our results have led to the discovery of an 
action, which apparently has hitherto escaped notice, by which methane is 
formed. Apart from theoretical interest the method would appear to have 
important technical possibilities, either as a means of producing pure methane 
or of enriching of town’s gas in methane, because by its use more methane is 
formed from water-gas than by other methods.
In order to make clear the course of the action about to be described it 
will be well briefly to enumerate some of the known interactions of carbon

monoxide and hydrogen on the one hand, and of the former gas and steam 
on the other.
The behaviour of carbon monoxide and excess of hydrogen over the tem­
perature range 230-400° C. at the surface of metallic catalysts has been 
exhaustively studied by Sabatier and his co-workers,* who observed that, 
whilst copper, iron and platinum were without action, nickel, cobalt and 
palladium induced the formation of methane according to the equation :
CO + 3H2 = CH4 + H20.
Above about 300° C. (but not markedly below about 400° C.) carbon monoxide 
also decomposes in presence of finely divided metals as follows :—
2CO = C + C02.
Whilst the above hydrogenation process is a useful laboratory means of 
synthesizing methane, it is open to the important technical objections that 
hydrogen is required in practice in excess of the amount given by the equation, 
and that in any case an equal volume of hydrogen must be added to the cheaper 
water-gas to provide the theoretical mixture of one volume of carbon monoxide 
and three volumes of hydrogen. Since this extra hydrogen must in general 
be made from water-gas, the loss in gas volume becomes considerable and 
the yield of methane is in practice only about 15 per cent, of the total water-gas 
required.
Sabatier therefore indicatedf conditions under which water-gas itself could 
be transformed into methane, or into the latter accompanied by hydrogen and 
carbon dioxide. This was effected by passing the gas over nickel at a rela­
tively high temperature, 400-500° C., when both actions of hydrogenation 
and carbonization occur, and the total change may be given as :—
3CO + 3H2 = CH4 + H20 + C + C02;
the deposited carbon is then exposed at the same temperature to a current 
of steam, which in presence of the nickel yields a mixture of hydrogen, methane 
and carbon dioxide and leaves the nickel ready for participation again in the 
first phase of the process.
Sabatier also pointed outj that both phases might be'united, a mixture of

He suggested 
that the following equation summarized the main action :—
5C0+5H2+ H 20 = 2CH4 + 2H2+3C 02.
This equation is, in effect, merely a summation of the following processes:—
r 3CO + 3H20 = 3C02 + 3H2.
I 2CO+ 6H2 - 2CH4 + 2H20.
This introduces another action, namely, that between carbon monoxide and 
steam in presence of reduced metals such as iron, copper, nickel, etc.
Whilst this process is well known to proceed, in the presence of iron or iron 
oxide, by alternate reduction of iron oxide by the carbon monoxide, and 
oxidation of iron (or ferrous oxide) by the steam, we have shown elsewhere* 
that prepared copper effects the same ultimate change:
CO + H 20 = C02 + H 2,
by an entirely different mechanism, namely, the decomposition of formic acid 
transiently produced from the carbon monoxide and steam.
The present communication deals with the behaviour of water-gas (purified 
from sulphur compounds, etc.) in presence of various finely divided metals 
other than copper at temperatures between 200° and 300° C.
Experiments were made in which the volume and composition of the gas 
before and after passage over the prepared metals was measured, and the 
approximate volumes of gases which had disappeared and those of the products 
were thus deduced.
It was considered possible, in the first place, that combination of carbon 
monoxide and hydrogen might occur so that formaldehyde or one of its poly- 
merides or transition products would be produced :
CO + H 2 = H . CHO ;
or, again, that the usual hydrogenation might take place, leaving excess of 
carbon monoxide unattacked:
3CO + 3Ha = CH4 + H 20 + 2CO.
In point of fact, neither of these take place in presence of nickel (except 
that towards 300° C. the latter sets in to a minor degree), the only action being 
one which has apparently hitherto escaped observation, namely,
2CO+2H2 = C02+CH4.
This action, although never complete, proceeds to a very considerable extent,

Ten volumes of water-gas of the composition 7-1 per cent. C02, 38-0

H2 and 41-0 per cent. CH4.
Thus 3-1 volumes CO and 3-8 volumes H 2 disappeared, producing 1-5 
volumes of C02 and 1-7 volumes of CH4.
Assuming that the excess of methane over carbon dioxide is due to normal 
hydrogenation, we may represent the action a s :
r 0-2 CO + 0-6 H2 = 0-2 H 20 + 0-2 CH4,
12*9 CO + 3-2 H2 = 1-5 C02 + 1-5 CH4,
or, to the nearest whole numbers,
2CO + 2H2 = C02 + CH4.
The “ oxidation ” of carbon monoxide to dioxide is somewhat paradoxical 
in view of the “ reducing ” conditions which obtain in the process, but it is 
very readily explained if our former work on copper* is considered in conjunc­
tion with the present investigation.
In the present experiments the gases were not dried and there would always 
be sufficient water present to initiate the action
CO + H20 -> (H . COOH) -> C02 + H 20,f 
which will be provoked by nickel at least as readily as by copper, and probably 
more readily, on the basis of general analogy between the activities of nickel 
and copper.
Consequently, if we consider two volumes of water-gas, 2CO + 2H2, the 
action may be expressed as
/ (i) CO + h 2o = c o 2 + h 2,
\(ii) CO + 2H2 + H 2 = CH4 + H20,
or 2CO + 2Ha = C02 + CH4.
It has not been possible to determine whether, in the rigorous absence of 
all moisture, this change would be suppressed (an argument which would 
definitely prove the mechanism of the process), because it is impossible to

Nevertheless, we are of opinion that this explanation is the most consistent 
with prior knowledge as well as the simplest of what at first appears to be a 
puzzling transformation.
Another possible explanation deserves some consideration, although the 
experimental evidence is against i t :—It is known* that aldehydes are, under 
certain conditions, polymerized to fatty acid esters in presence of finely divided 
metals. Thus it might be supposed that the following changes take place, 
methyl formate formed from formaldehyde breaking down into carbon dioxide 
and methane:—
2CO+2H, -> (2H. CHO) -> (H . COOCH3) -> C02+CH4.
Against this must be set the fact that we have been unable to detect the 
slightest trace of either of these compounds. A large volume of the gases 
emerging from the catalyst has been thoroughly scrubbed through a small 
quantity of water and the solution carefully examined. 
The solution exerts 
some slight reducing action on ammoniacal silver nitrate and on mercuric 
chloride, as in the absence of any catalyst,f but in no instance was the iodoform 
test responded to, as would have been the case in presence of traces of formal­
dehyde ; further, careful fractionation through an 8-pear Young-Thomas 
column revealed no trace of any liquid boiling below 100° C. (methyl formate 
or methyl alcohol).
The trace of water-soluble matter in the gas produced is thus exactly similar 
to that formed when water-gas and steam are passed over prepared copper, 
i-e., it answers to tests characteristic of formic acid but not to those which 
would indicate formaldehyde or methyl alcohol.
We have confirmed Sabatier’s observationsJ that formaldehyde is reduced to 
methyl alcohol in presence of hydrogen and nickel (when it also suffers partial 
decomposition into carbon monoxide and hydrogen), but find that methyl 
alcohol is not converted to methane under similar conditions.
Another factor is that, so far as we have been able to ascertain, there is no>

experimental evidence to be obtained that hydrogenation of carbon monoxide 
or dioxide goes in successive stages. As already mentioned, with carbon 
monoxide and hydrogen no indication has been given, either at the low est 
temperature of hydrogenation or under other conditions, that either formal­
dehyde or methyl alcohol are produced :
CO+H2 -> H . CHO+H2 
CH3OH+H2 ■> c h4+ h 2o.
Methane appears to be produced alone in the actual hydrogenation process, 
except for the change discussed in this paper when the hydrogen is reduced 
to an equal volume with the carbon monoxide.
Similarly, when carbon dioxide and hydrogen are passed over the catalyst 
no sign of the above compounds nor of carbon monoxide has appeared, as 
would be expected in a reduction by stages.
Indeed, in the case of carbon dioxide we have passed equal volumes of this 
gas and hydrogen over prepared nickel and have observed only consumption 
of the hydrogen with production of methane, leaving excess of carbon dioxide 
untouched :
4C02 + 4H2 - 3C02 + CH4 + 2H20.
The gas changes produced in two experiments may be quoted in illustration 
of this :—
(a) with equal volumes of carbon dioxide and hydrogen at 255° C., 1
volume of carbon dioxide and 4 • 1 volumes of hydrogen disappeared, 
whilst 0 • 9 volumes of methane were observed to have been 
produced ;
(b) with an original mixture of 1 volume of carbon dioxide and 2 volumes
of hydrogen at 250° C., 1 volume of carbon dioxide and 3-7 volumes 
of hydrogen disappeared, whilst 1*1 volumes of methane were 
observed to have been produced.
Consequently we consider that the actual hydrogenation process proceeds 
direct from carbon dioxide or monoxide to methane and water.
The action between equal volumes of carbon monoxide and hydrogen in 
presence of nickel or similar catalyst at temperatures below 300° C. is, however, 
mainly
2CO + 2H2 = C02 + CH4,
and we consider that this is due to one molecule of the monoxide and a molecule 
of water interacting and yielding a molecule each of carbon dioxide and of 
hydrogen—the latter, with the balance of hydrogen present, furnishing sufficient

hydrogen for the normal hydrogenation of a second molecule of carbon 
monoxide.
It is somewhat singular that this action has escaped notice previously. 
Nickel is the most efficient catalyst of those which we have examined ; cobalt 
is also quite active (but apparently in a somewhat different direction). 
The 
change commences at about 180° C., somewhat lower than with nickel. This 
is another instance of the fact, which we have previously noted,* that until 
the temperature rises well above the stability limit of nickel carbonyl (180° C.) 
the latter complex is not sufficiently “ unstable 55 for catalytic action to proceed 
freely.
In the case of cobalt the normal hydrogenation
CO + 3H2 = CH4 + H20 
preponderates, and the carbonizing action
2CO = C + C02
also appears to take place to a considerable extent, so that the action
2CO + 2H2 - C02 + CH4
is here a subsidiary one.
Silver is inert, iron nearly so, whilst platinum and palladium are of minor 
activity in the present action.
The following mixed catalysts were also studied : copper-nickel, iron-nickel, 
cobalt-nickel, cobalt-platinum and cobalt-palladium. In all cases it was 
found that the action was less vigorous than when the corresponding single 
catalyst (cobalt or nickel) was employed.
At increased pressures (up to 6 atmospheres) the process proceeds much 
as at atmospheric pressure, except that in the case of nickel the minimum 
temperature of interaction rises with increasing pressure (i.e., with increasing 
stability of nickel carbonyl at any given temperature),
We conclude this communication with some examples of the change effected 
with nickel or cobalt at varying temperatures and pressures :—
I. Approximately equal volumes of carbon monoxide and hydrogen passed over 
prepared nickel.
(i) At 280° C. and atmospheric pressure :
3*99 vols. CO + 3*95 vols. H2 disappeared and 1-79 vols. C02 + 1*78 
vols. CH4 were produced 
(or, 2CO + 2H2 = 0-9 C02 + 0*9 vols. CH4).

At 180° C. and atmospheric pressure:

vols. CH4 were produced.
In this case the main action is evidently
CO + 3H2 = CH4 + H20,
whilst carbonization also occurred in spite of the low temperature of the 
experiment.
The process 2CO + 2H2 = C02 + CH4 does not appear to proceed so 
readily with cobalt as with nickel.
It should be remarked that whilst the earlier investigators appear to have 
directed their attention mainly to the alteration in composition of gases by 
passage over a catalyst, we have endeavoured to obtain quantitative data by 
observing in addition the contraction undergone by the gas during the process..

Under the conditions of our experiments, this involved differential readings 
between two gas-meters with gas flowing at from 25 to 100 litres per hour.
These measurements involve a possible maximum meter error of perhaps 
2 per cent. ; in addition, the analytical determination of a mixture of hydrogen 
and methane is open to small errors (eliminated, of course, as far as possible 
by duplicate analyses). 
Since the alterations in gas-volumes deduced from 
these data are also based on differences, any of the above experimental errors, 
if present, will have a cumulative effect on the final result.
It is therefore unreasonable to expect, in work of this character, an exact 
experimental accordance between the volumes of gases which have interacted ; 
nevertheless, the data we have given are a sufficiently close approximation to 
establish that, in the case of nickel at all events, equal volumes of carbon 
monoxide and hydrogen are transformed into a mixture of carbon dioxide and 
methane from 200° C. upwards.
This process may prove of value in gas practice since the proportion of 
methane is 25 per cent, of the water-gas decomposed, whereas by any of the 
other processes referred to earlier in this paper the maximum possible amount 
is only 20 per cent.
The large amount of carbon monoxide in town’s gas as at present manufac­
tured has met with criticism, notably from Prof. W. A. Bone ; this could be 
reduced by a partial application of the present process if it were technically 
feasible to remove the carbon dioxide simultaneously formed. 
Thus, the 
elimination of half the carbon monoxide present in fresh water-gas by this 
method causes a total gas-contraction of about 30-40 per cent, after the carbon 
dioxide produced has been removed.
On the other hand, if it were desired to manufacture pure methane the 
process would be repeated, the carbon dioxide produced being absorbed until 
only small proportions of carbon monoxide and hydrogen were left. In an 
actual experiment, after two passages of the gas over nickel at 240-250° C. 
and removal of carbon dioxide from the treated gas each time, the product 
contained 0*8 per cent. C02, 0*9 per cent. CO, 8*5 per cent. H2 and 77-7 
per cent. CH4.
Passage of this gas over heated copper oxide produced a sample containing 
3 • 8 per cent. C02, nil CO, 1 • 9 per cent. H2 and 82 • 6 per cent. CH4 ; to obtain 
pure methane this product is then fractionated at a low temperature, in order 
to eliminate nitrogen accumulated from the original water-gas and any 
remaining traces of hydrogen.
The method renders the preparation of pure methane in quantity very

III.— The Colours o f Labrador Felspar.
By Lord R ayleigh, F.R.S.
(Received January 25, 1923.)
[Plate 1.]
§ 1. Introduction.
The brilliant colours displayed by reflexion at certain angles from a polished 
surface of labradorite, or Labrador felspar, have long been known, and 
specimens of the material are to be seen in most mineral collections. Several 
investigations of the origin of these colours have been published,* but I must 
confess that I have not been able to get clear ideas by studying them. 
The 
writers approach the subject primarily from the mineralogist's point of view, 
and much mineralogical detail is introduced which seems doubtfully relevant 
and (to me at least) difficult to follow.
Vogelsang’s conclusion (translated) is: “ The results of my investigations, 
so far as they concern the various colourations of labradorite, may be 
summarised as follows: A blue reflexion, due to a polarisation effect, is
peculiar to a certain crystalline condition of the mineral. 
A golden yellow 
results from total reflexion on the included microlites, which consist of 
magnetic oxide of iron or of diallage as well; the association of these
